engage.hook: How does the Sun appear to move across the sky during a single day?
engage.content: You have watched sunrise and sunset your whole life. Predict the path the Sun takes from morning to night, then we will explain what is really moving.
engage.imageDescription: time-lapse photograph of the Sun arcing across the sky from sunrise to sunset

learn.heading: Day and night, and a year

items: The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours.
The side facing the Sun has day; the side facing away has night.
The Earth spins from west to east, so the Sun appears to rise in the east.
The Earth orbits the Sun once every 365.25 days.
One full orbit is one year.
The extra quarter day is why we add a leap day every four years.

learn.imageDescription: diagram of Earth spinning on its tilted axis while orbiting the Sun

learn.heading: The Earth's tilt and the seasons

items: The Earth is tilted on its axis by about 23.5 degrees.
In summer your hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, giving longer, warmer days.
In winter it tilts away, giving shorter, colder days.
When the northern hemisphere has summer, the southern hemisphere has winter.

learn.imageDescription: diagram showing Earth's axial tilt causing seasons in the northern and southern hemispheres

build.q: What causes day and night on Earth?
options: The Sun orbits the Earth once a day
The Earth spins on its axis once a day
The Moon blocks the Sun's light
The Earth orbits the Sun once a day
build.explanation: The Earth spins on its axis every 24 hours, so one side faces the Sun (day) and the other faces away (night).

build.q: Why does the Sun appear to rise in the east and set in the west?
options: The Sun moves around the Earth
The Earth spins from west to east
The Sun gets brighter then fades
build.explanation: The Earth rotates from west to east, so the Sun appears to travel the opposite way across the sky.

build.q: How long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
build.explanation: One orbit of the Sun takes 365.25 days, which is one year.

build.q: Why is it summer in Australia when it is winter in the UK?
options: Australia is much closer to the Sun
The two hemispheres tilt in opposite directions
Australia spins faster than the UK
The Sun only shines on Australia
build.explanation: The Earth's tilt means when the northern hemisphere leans away from the Sun (our winter), the southern hemisphere leans towards it (their summer).

developing.q: Why is it light during the daytime and dark at night?
developing.a: The Earth spins on its axis. The side facing the Sun has daylight; the side facing away is in shadow, giving night.

developing.q: Why does the Sun seem to rise in the east and set in the west?
developing.a: The Earth rotates from west to east, so the Sun appears to move the opposite way across the sky.

reaching.q: Why is it lunchtime in Australia when it is midnight in the UK?
reaching.a: They are on opposite sides of the Earth. The Sun lights only one half at a time, so when the UK faces away Australia faces the Sun.

reaching.q: Why does the Sun set later in summer than in winter?
reaching.a: In summer the UK tilts towards the Sun, so we spend longer in sunlight each day, giving longer days.

mastering.q: Why do Australians have a summer barbecue at Christmas while the UK builds snowmen?
mastering.a: Australia is in the southern hemisphere. When the north tilts away from the Sun (our winter), the south tilts towards it, giving them summer.

mastering.q: Explain why a day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.
mastering.a: Venus spins very slowly. It takes 243 Earth days to spin once (its day) but only 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun (its year).

Describe how the Moon changes its appearance during its orbit

questions.q: Explain why we have day and night.
questions.a: The Earth spins on its axis every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the side facing away has night.

questions.q: Explain why we have a year.
questions.a: The Earth takes 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once, which is one year.

questions.q: How long does the Earth take to spin once on its axis?
Which force keeps the Earth in orbit around the Sun?

engage.hook: Why does the Moon seem to change shape through the month?
engage.content: The Moon looks different night to night, from a thin sliver to a full circle. Predict what is really changing before we model it.
engage.imageDescription: composite photograph of the eight phases of the Moon across one month

learn.heading: The Moon and its phases

items: The Moon does not make its own light.
We see it because it reflects light from the Sun.
We only see the part of the sunlit Moon that faces the Earth.
The Moon orbits the Earth once every 28 days.
As it moves, we see different amounts of its sunlit side.
These different views are called the phases of the Moon.

learn.imageDescription: diagram of the Moon orbiting the Earth with the Sun lighting one side and the eight phases labelled

learn.heading: New Moon
learn.instruction: This is the view of the Moon from Earth.
learn.tip: The Moon sits between the Earth and the Sun, so the side facing us is dark.

learn.heading: Waxing Crescent
learn.instruction: This is the view of the Moon from Earth.
learn.tip: Waxing means the lit part is growing.

learn.heading: First Quarter
learn.instruction: This is the view of the Moon from Earth.
learn.tip: We can now see the right half lit.

learn.heading: Waxing Gibbous
learn.instruction: This is the view of the Moon from Earth.
learn.tip: More than half is lit and still growing.

learn.heading: Full Moon
learn.instruction: This is the view of the Moon from Earth.
learn.tip: The whole face we see is lit by the Sun.

learn.heading: Waning Gibbous
learn.instruction: This is the view of the Moon from Earth.
learn.tip: Waning means the lit part is shrinking.

learn.heading: Last Quarter
learn.instruction: This is the view of the Moon from Earth.
learn.tip: We can now see the left half lit.

learn.heading: Waning Crescent
learn.instruction: This is the view of the Moon from Earth.
learn.tip: Only a thin sliver is left before the next new Moon.

learn.heading: The far side of the Moon

items: The Moon spins once for every orbit of the Earth.
This means the same side always faces us.
The side we never see is called the far side, not the dark side.
Both sides get sunlight during the Moon's orbit.

learn.imageDescription: diagram showing the Moon keeping the same face towards Earth as it orbits

build.q: Why can we see the Moon in the night sky?
options: It reflects light from the Sun
It is a burning ball of gas
It reflects light from the Earth
build.explanation: The Moon does not make its own light. We see the sunlight it reflects.

build.q: How long does the Moon take to orbit the Earth?
build.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth once about every 28 days.

build.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
options: The Moon does not spin at all
The Moon spins once for each orbit of the Earth
The Moon is too far to see the other side
The far side is always in darkness
build.explanation: The Moon spins once for every orbit, so the same side always faces the Earth.

build.q: What force keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth?
build.explanation: Gravity is the force that keeps the Moon orbiting the Earth.

developing.q: The Moon does not make its own light. How can we see it?
developing.a: It reflects light from the Sun.

developing.q: How long does the Moon take to orbit the Earth?
Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
developing.a: The Moon spins once for every orbit, so the same side always faces us.

developing.q: What force keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth?

reaching.q: Why do we only see a full Moon once a month?
reaching.a: Only once each orbit is the Moon in the position where the whole side facing us is fully lit by the Sun.
When the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, so the side facing us gets no sunlight and looks dark.

reaching.q: Put the phases in order, starting from new Moon.
reaching.a: New Moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full Moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

mastering.q: Write a paragraph explaining why we see different phases of the Moon.
mastering.a: As the Moon orbits the Earth we see different amounts of its sunlit side, from none at new Moon to all at full Moon and back again.

mastering.q: Explain why the Moon's far side is not actually always dark.
mastering.a: The Moon spins once per orbit so one side always faces away from Earth, but that far side still receives sunlight during the orbit.

learn.heading: Finite and renewable resources

items: Resources are taken from the atmosphere, the water and the land.
We turn them into useful materials and products.
Finite resources will run out, for example coal, oil and slate.
Renewable resources can be replaced, for example wood and biogas.
Recycling makes finite resources last longer.

learn.imageDescription: comparison of finite resources such as coal and oil with renewable resources such as wood

What each material is turned into

questions.q: Name two materials that are sorted for recycling.
questions.a: Any two: glass, metal, paper, plastic.

questions.q: Give one reason recycling is better than making a material from new.
questions.a: It saves finite raw materials and uses less energy.

build.q: Which of these is a renewable resource?
build.explanation: Wood is renewable because we can grow more trees. Coal, oil and slate are finite.

build.q: Why does recycling help finite resources last longer?
options: It reduces how quickly we use up raw materials
It removes the need for any energy
build.explanation: Recycling reuses materials, so we take less new resource from the ground.

build.q: Aluminium lasts about 1780 years now, or 2225 years if we cut use by 25%. What does this show?
options: Using less makes a resource last longer
build.explanation: Reducing use and recycling both extend how long a finite resource lasts.

build.q: Where are the Earth's resources extracted from?
build.explanation: Resources come from the atmosphere, the water and the land.

developing.q: Sort these into finite or renewable: coal, wood, oil, biogas.
developing.a: Finite: coal, oil. Renewable: wood, biogas.

developing.q: Name two materials that we commonly recycle.
developing.a: Any two: glass, metal, paper, plastic.
It saves finite resources, uses less energy, or reduces waste.

reaching.q: Describe how one material, such as glass or metal, is recycled.
reaching.a: It is collected, sorted, cleaned, melted down and then reshaped into new products.

reaching.q: Give one problem with recycling a material.
reaching.a: Sorting and cleaning cost money and energy, and some materials lose quality each time.

mastering.q: Use the resource data to write a short speech persuading people to recycle.
mastering.a: Use figures like copper having about 14 years left, and argue recycling extends supplies, saves energy and cuts waste.

mastering.q: Evaluate the pros and cons of recycling metal.
mastering.a: Pros: it saves finite ore and energy. Cons: collection and sorting cost money and energy. Overall it makes limited supplies last longer.
